Lessons.Title: Different Types of Sequences
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: compare, distinguish and generate arithmetic and geometric sequences from tables, graphs, function notation and numerical patterns.
Warm-up: evaluate a function of the form f(n)=3n-7 at specified integer inputs; explain the role of the input n rather than confusing it with the term value.

Discuss three distinct examples: A=30,40,50,60,70 is arithmetic (+10); B=0,5,15,30,50 has growing differences (+5,+10,+15,+20); C=1,2,4,8,16 is geometric (times two). The same first terms do not guarantee the same type of growth.
With continuation of those rules to term 10, A(10)=120, B(10)=225 and C(10)=512. The nonlinear B value is second largest; do not choose based on the appearance of only the first five terms.
Arithmetic rule: from a starting term a(1), a(n)=a(1)+(n-1)d. Geometric rule: from starting term g(1), g(n)=g(1)r^(n-1). Both require an explicit starting index.
A positive constant sequence such as 5,5,5,... has common difference zero and common ratio one. It is both arithmetic and geometric; this is an exception to an informal either/or classification.

Compare a table and a graph of the same sequence carefully. If the input positions skip integers, multiplying successive listed output values does not prove a constant multiplier from n to n+1. Teacher reviews the graph, its domain, axes and argument.

Practice: fill missing arithmetic terms with signed or fractional differences, find geometric factors, distinguish 'neither', and supply a valid continuation for an arithmetic, geometric or nonstandard rule.

Independent cool-down (Edulytics): compare U=4,10,16,22 and V=4,10,25,62.5. Decide which is arithmetic and which is geometric, state a recursive rule, and predict the next term. Justify using consecutive differences or ratios.

KeyConcepts.Title: Arithmetic sequence
KeyConcepts.Definition: One constant amount is added at each step.

KeyConcepts.Title: Geometric sequence
KeyConcepts.Definition: One constant factor multiplies consecutive nonzero terms.

KeyConcepts.Title: Neither or both
KeyConcepts.Definition: Not all sequences fit either classification, while positive constant sequences fit both.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check at least two differences and two well-defined adjacent ratios.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare term 10 in three patterns
WorkedExamples.Question: Which has the second-largest 10th term: 30,40,50,...; 0,5,15,30,50,...; or 1,2,4,8,16,...?
WorkedExamples.Method: Identify a separate rule for each sequence.
WorkedExamples.Check: B has nonconstant differences and is neither arithmetic nor geometric.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find an unknown arithmetic rate
WorkedExamples.Question: Fill -3,-2,_,_,1 and give the common difference.
Steps: The following term 1 verifies a constant +1.

WorkedExamples.Title: A sequence that fits two definitions
WorkedExamples.Question: Can a positive constant sequence such as 7,7,7,... be arithmetic and geometric?
Steps: Both differences and ratios are constant.
WorkedExamples.Check: This example refutes a claim that the categories never overlap.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Deciding a sequence is geometric after observing one ratio.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A common ratio must be maintained at each step.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check every available consecutive nonzero pair.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Equating a nonlinear sequence with arithmetic because the terms increase.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Increasing differences are not a common difference.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming a positive constant sequence cannot be both.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: It has difference zero and ratio one.

SummaryPoints: Arithmetic: constant difference; geometric: constant ratio.
Some sequences are neither, and positive constant sequences are both.
Term indices are discrete; source graphs need justified axis and step interpretation.
Teacher checks the open classification argument and graphs.
